title: How NYC Open Mics Work: Sign-Ups, Costs & Times
excerpt: Bucket vs list sign-up, drink minimums, how early to arrive and what to expect at your first NYC open mic.
metaDescription: Bucket vs list sign-up, what a two item minimum means, how early to arrive and what NYC open mics cost. A practical guide for first-time comedians.
author: Adam Malev
body:
If you have never done an open mic in New York, the listings can be confusing. One says bucket. Another says list. A third says two item minimum, which sounds like a tax form. None of it explains what you actually do when you walk in the door.

Here is how comedy open mics in NYC work in practice.

## Bucket sign-up versus list sign-up

Almost every open mic uses one of two systems, and the difference decides when you should show up.

A bucket mic means everyone writes their name on a slip of paper and drops it in a bucket, hat or jar. The host draws names at random. Arriving early does not get you an earlier slot, it only guarantees you are in the draw before it closes. What matters is being there before the bucket is pulled.

A list mic is first come, first served. You write your name on a sheet and you go up in that order. Here arriving early matters a great deal. At popular list mics, comics turn up an hour before the posted start time to get a slot near the top, because the room empties out as the night goes on and the last few spots perform to almost nobody.

If a listing does not say which system a mic uses, assume list and arrive early. That mistake costs you nothing. The reverse mistake costs you the spot.

## What open mics in NYC cost

Of 417 comedy open mics listed on Comediq across New York, the Hudson Valley, Los Angeles and Austin, 128 are free. The most common price is five dollars. That is the honest answer to a question most beginners get wrong, because the advice circulating secondhand suggests New York is more expensive than it is.

The prices that look confusing are usually not prices at all. A one-drink minimum means you perform for free but have to buy one drink, which is a bar covering its costs for giving up a room on a slow night. A two-item minimum is the same idea with two purchases, usually at comedy clubs rather than bars, and it can mean food or drink. A few mics ask for a cash amount plus one item, which is a club charging for stage time and the bar charging separately.

Cash still matters. Plenty of NYC mics are cash only at the door, so bring small bills even when a listing shows a card-friendly venue.

## How early to arrive

For a list mic, thirty to sixty minutes before the posted start time is normal at busy rooms. For a bucket mic, arriving fifteen minutes early is usually enough, as long as you are there for the draw.

The posted time on any listing is the show time, not the sign-up time. Sign-up often opens an hour earlier and closes when the room is full. This single detail is the most common reason new comics show up and find they cannot get on.

## How long you get on stage

Most NYC open mics give between three and five minutes. Some bucket mics drop to two or three minutes when turnout is heavy, because the host has to fit everybody in. A handful of mics offer longer sets, usually seven minutes, and those tend to be harder to get into.

Set length is not fixed. It is decided by how many people show up that night. Prepare for the shorter end of the range, and you will never be the comic who gets the light early and has no ending ready.

## Do you need to be experienced?

No. Open mics exist specifically so that people can try material in front of a room. The audience at most NYC mics is other comedians waiting their turn, which is a tougher crowd than a real show but a far more forgiving one for a first attempt. Nobody there expects polish.

Some mics are explicitly [beginner-friendly](/beginner-friendly) and lower pressure than others. Those are worth starting with.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is bucket sign-up at an open mic?

Bucket sign-up means every comic writes their name on a slip and the host draws names at random to set the order. Arriving early does not improve your position, but you must be present before the draw closes.

### Do you have to pay to perform at open mics in NYC?

Not always. Of 417 mics listed on Comediq, 128 are [free](/free-mics). The most common price is five dollars, and many of the rest ask for a one-drink or two-item minimum rather than a cash fee.

### What does a two-item minimum mean at a comedy club?

It means you need to buy two items, usually food or drinks, to perform or attend. It is how the venue covers its costs rather than a charge for stage time.

### How early should you arrive at an NYC open mic?

For list mics, thirty to sixty minutes before the posted time. For bucket mics, around fifteen minutes before, provided you are there for the draw. The posted time is the show time, not the sign-up time.

### How long is a set at an NYC open mic?

Usually three to five minutes. It can drop to two or three minutes on busy nights, because the host adjusts set length to fit everyone who turns up.

### What night has the most open mics in New York?

[Wednesday](/open-mics/wednesday) is the busiest night across the city, though mics run every night of the week in all five boroughs.

## Find a mic

You can browse every [open mic currently running in New York](/open-mics) by night of the week or by borough, with the cost, sign-up method, and start time listed for each one.

Start with [Manhattan](/open-mics/manhattan), [Brooklyn](/open-mics/brooklyn) or [Queens](/open-mics/queens).

title: Open Mic Etiquette: What NYC Comics Wish You Knew
excerpt: Staying for other comics, respecting your time limit, handling the mic, and the mistakes that get you quietly remembered.
metaDescription: The unwritten rules of NYC comedy open mics: staying for other comics, respecting your time limit, handling the mic and what to do before your first set.
author: Adam Malev
body:
Nobody tells you the rules at an open mic because everyone assumes you already know them. You do not, and neither did they on their first night. Here is what experienced comics in New York expect from the room, and the mistakes that get you quietly remembered for the wrong reasons.

## Stay for other comics

This is the single biggest unwritten rule at comedy open mics, and breaking it is the fastest way to get a reputation.

If you perform and leave, you are treating the room as an audience for yourself while giving nothing back. At a typical NYC mic, the crowd is almost entirely other comedians, so everyone who walks out makes the room worse for whoever is next. Hosts notice. Other comics notice.

Stay for at least a few sets after yours. Stay for the whole thing when you can. Comics who stay get invited to things.

## Respect your time limit

Most NYC open mics give three to five minutes. When the host flashes the light, you have roughly thirty seconds to finish. Not thirty seconds to start a new bit.

Going over your time is not a sign of confidence. It takes time directly from the comics after you, and at a mic running thirty names deep, it can mean someone does not get up at all. Hosts remember who runs long. It is the most common reason a comic stops getting booked.

Time your set at home. Out loud, with a timer. It is always longer than you think.

## Handle the microphone properly

Take the mic out of the stand at the start and move the stand aside. Hand the mic back at the end. Do this once, smoothly, without a struggle.

Fumbling the mic stand for twenty seconds burns a chunk of a five-minute set and reads as unprepared. Practise it at home with a hairbrush if you have to. Nobody will know.

## Do not heckle, even as a joke

In a room full of comedians, the temptation to shout something funny is real. Resist it. You are not helping, and the person on stage is trying to work out whether a joke lands, which they cannot do if the room is reacting to you instead.

The same applies to loud talking at the back, scrolling with your screen brightness up, and laughing at your friend's table rather than the stage.

## Laugh honestly

You are not obliged to fake laughter, and experienced comics can tell when a laugh is polite. But sitting in stony silence at a mic because you are rehearsing your own set in your head is also a choice, and it makes the room harder for everyone.

Listen properly. Laugh when something is funny. That is the whole ask.

## Know the room before you book it

Mics differ. Some are brand new comics working out their first jokes. Some are working comics tightening material for paid spots. Some have a specific audience, such as women and nonbinary rooms or LGBTQ rooms, and turning up without knowing that is a bad look.

Check what kind of room it is before you sign up. Watching one before you perform at it is the best preparation there is. If you are starting out, the [beginner-friendly](/beginner-friendly) rooms are the easier place to begin.

## Pay what the room asks

Of 417 open mics listed on Comediq, 128 are [free](/free-mics). The rest ask for something, usually five dollars or a one-drink minimum. That is a venue covering its costs for giving up a room on a slow night.

Pay it without complaint, and bring cash because many NYC mics are cash only. Trying to perform without buying the drink at a bar mic is how rooms get cancelled.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is it rude to leave an open mic after your set?

Yes, and it is the most commonly cited breach of open mic etiquette. The audience at most mics is other comedians, so leaving early makes the room worse for the people after you. Stay for at least a few sets.

### What happens if you go over your time at an open mic?

The host will light you, meaning they signal that your time is nearly up. Ignoring it takes time from the comics after you and is the quickest way to stop getting spots at that room.

### Can you record your set at an open mic?

Usually yes, but ask the host first. Audio recording from a phone on a table is normally fine. Setting up cameras or tripods is not, and some rooms do not allow recording at all.

### What should you wear to an open mic?

Whatever you would wear to a bar. There is no dress code at NYC open mics, and dressing up marks you as new more than anything you say on stage.

### Should you tell the room it is your first open mic?

Opinions differ. It can buy goodwill from other comics who remember their own first night, but it can also read as asking for a pass. Most experienced comics advise just doing your jokes.

### Do you have to buy a drink at an open mic?

At mics with a one-drink or two-item minimum, yes. That is the arrangement that lets the venue host the room, and not honouring it is how mics lose their venues.

## Find a room

You can browse every [open mic running in New York](/open-mics) by night or by borough, with the cost, sign-up method and start time for each one.

Start with [Manhattan](/open-mics/manhattan), [Brooklyn](/open-mics/brooklyn) or [Queens](/open-mics/queens).

title: NYC Open Mic Report: Where and When Mics Run
excerpt: Manhattan has 192 open mics and the Bronx has one. Where open mics run in New York, which nights are busiest, and where the free rooms are.
metaDescription: Of 302 NYC open mics, Manhattan has 192 and the Bronx has one. Queens is 82% free, Manhattan 12%. Where and when open mics run in New York.
author: Adam Malev
body:
Comediq currently lists 418 comedy open mics across New York, the Hudson Valley, Los Angeles and Austin. 128 of them are free, the most common price is five dollars, and Wednesday is the busiest night.

Those are the headline numbers. The breakdown underneath them is more interesting, and it says things about the New York comedy scene that are hard to notice from inside it.

## Where the open mics are

There are 302 open mics across the five boroughs of New York City. They are not spread evenly.

Manhattan has 192. Brooklyn has 90. Queens has 17. Staten Island has two. The Bronx has one.

That is not a gentle gradient. Manhattan has nearly two thirds of every open mic in the city, and Brooklyn has almost all of the rest. A comic living in the Bronx has a single mic in their borough and a subway ride to everything else.

## The free mics are where the mics are not

This is the finding that surprised me most, because it runs opposite to what you would expect.

Manhattan has 192 open mics and only 24 of them are free, around 12 percent. Brooklyn has 90 mics and 33 are free, around 37 percent. Queens has 17 mics and 14 of them are free, which is 82 percent.

So the borough with the fewest open mics has, by a wide margin, the highest proportion of free ones. The borough with the most charges for almost all of them.

The reason is structural rather than sinister. Manhattan mics are concentrated at dedicated comedy clubs with rent to cover, and those clubs charge for stage time. Queens mics run at bars, coffee shops and community spaces that are giving away a quiet weeknight rather than selling a product.

For a comic on a budget, that changes the calculation. The cheap stage time is not in the places with the most stage time.

## When the open mics run

Open mics listed on Comediq by night of the week:

Wednesday has 80, Tuesday 77, Thursday 71, Monday 62, Friday 49, Sunday 47, and Saturday 32.

Midweek dominates. Tuesday through Thursday accounts for 228 of 418 mics, which is around 55 percent of everything in three nights.

Saturday is the worst night for stage time by a long way, with 32 mics, and only five of those are free. That makes sense once you remember who open mics are for. Weekends belong to booked shows with paying audiences. Rooms are only available to comics when nobody is paying to sit in them.

If you can get out one night a week, make it a Wednesday. If you can get out three, Tuesday through Thursday gives you the most choice and the most free options.

## What this means if you are starting out

Build your week around midweek nights, because that is when the rooms exist.

If cost is your constraint, look at Brooklyn and Queens before Manhattan. The free rooms are concentrated there, and 72 of the 302 NYC mics are free in total.

If you live in the Bronx or Staten Island, accept early that you are travelling. There is no local scene to build a habit around, and pretending otherwise just leads to going out less.

## Frequently asked questions

### How many open mics are there in NYC?

There are 302 comedy open mics across the five boroughs currently listed on Comediq. Manhattan has 192, Brooklyn has 90, Queens has 17, Staten Island has two and the Bronx has one.

### Which NYC borough has the most free open mics?

Brooklyn has the most free mics by count, with 33. Queens has the highest proportion, with 14 of its 17 mics free. Manhattan has the most mics overall but only 24 free ones.

### What night has the most comedy open mics?

Wednesday, with 80 mics listed. Tuesday has 77 and Thursday has 71. Midweek accounts for more than half of all open mics.

### What is the quietest night for open mics?

Saturday, with 32 mics, only five of which are free. Weekend nights are given over to booked shows rather than open mics.

### Are there open mics in the Bronx or Staten Island?

Barely. The Bronx has one listed open mic and Staten Island has two. Comics in those boroughs generally travel to Manhattan or Brooklyn.

### How much do NYC open mics cost?

The most common price is five dollars. Across all 418 mics listed, 128 are free. Many of the rest ask for a one drink or two item minimum rather than a cash fee.

## Browse the mics

You can see every [open mic](/open-mics) by borough or by night, with the cost, sign-up method and start time for each one, and filter to [free mics](/free-mics) only.

Start with [Manhattan](/open-mics/manhattan), [Brooklyn](/open-mics/brooklyn), [Queens](/open-mics/queens) or [Wednesday](/open-mics/wednesday).

title: Free Comedy in NYC: What You Can Watch for Nothing
excerpt: 128 free open mics run across New York every week. What they are like to watch, where the free rooms are, and which nights to go.
metaDescription: 128 free comedy open mics run across New York every week. What they are actually like to watch, which nights are busiest, and how free comedy in NYC works.
author: Adam Malev
body:
Search for free comedy in New York and most of what you find is not free. The guides say cheap, which usually means a five dollar ticket plus a two drink minimum, so you are out thirty dollars before you have laughed at anything.

There is genuinely free live comedy in this city, most nights of the week, in every borough except two. It just is not the kind of show most people are picturing, and whether it is right for you depends entirely on what you want from an evening.

Here is the honest version.

## Free comedy in NYC means open mics

Of the 418 comedy open mics listed on Comediq, 128 are free to attend. No ticket, no cover, no minimum. You walk in, sit down and watch.

An open mic is where comedians try out new material. Some of it is good. Some of it is being said out loud for the first time and dies in front of you. The person on stage is usually working, not performing in the sense you would expect at a club.

That is the whole trade. You pay nothing, and in exchange you see comedy before anyone has decided whether it works.

## What a free open mic is actually like

The audience at most New York open mics is other comedians waiting for their turn. That means the room is attentive but quiet. People laugh at craft rather than at jokes, and a bit that bombs still gets a nod from the back.

Sets run three to five minutes, so you will see a lot of different people in an hour. Some rooms run thirty names deep.

If you arrive expecting a polished lineup, you will be disappointed. If you arrive curious about how comedy gets made, it is one of the more interesting nights out in the city, and occasionally you watch someone try something for the first time that is genuinely great.

## Where the free rooms are

Free comedy is not spread evenly across New York.

Brooklyn has the most free open mics, with 33. Queens has 14, which is 82 percent of every mic in the borough. Manhattan has 192 open mics in total but only 24 of them are free, because Manhattan rooms are mostly at comedy clubs with rent to cover.

The Bronx has one open mic and it is free. Staten Island has two and neither is.

So if you want to watch comedy for nothing, Brooklyn and Queens are where to look. The bars and coffee shops running these rooms are giving away a quiet weeknight rather than selling tickets.

## Which nights to go

Wednesday has the most open mics of any night at 80, followed by Tuesday at 77 and Thursday at 71.

Saturday is the worst night by a wide margin, with 32 mics and only five of them free. Weekends belong to ticketed shows with paying audiences, so free comedy is a midweek thing.

If you are choosing a night at random, go on a Wednesday.

## How to behave if you go

Open mics are working rooms, so a few things matter.

Sit down, put your phone away and actually watch. A room with three people staring at screens is noticeably harder to perform in.

Laugh when something is funny and do not laugh politely when it is not. Comics are reading the room to find out what works, and fake laughter gives them bad information.

Do not heckle. Not even helpfully.

If the venue is a bar, buy a drink even when the mic is free. That is the arrangement keeping the room open.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is there free comedy in New York City?

Yes. 128 of the 418 comedy open mics listed on Comediq are free to attend, with no ticket or minimum. They run most nights of the week, concentrated in Brooklyn and Queens.

### Can anyone watch a comedy open mic?

Yes. Open mics are open to the public, and you do not need to perform or sign up to attend. Most of the audience will be other comedians, but nobody will stop you watching.

### Are free comedy shows in NYC any good?

It depends what you want. Open mics are comedians testing new material, so the quality varies enormously within a single night. It is not a polished showcase, but it is free and you see a lot of different performers in an hour.

### What is the difference between an open mic and a comedy show?

An open mic is unbooked and anyone can sign up to perform, usually for three to five minutes. A comedy show has a booked lineup of comics performing material they have already worked out, and almost always costs money.

### Which night has the most free comedy in NYC?

Wednesday, with 80 open mics running citywide. Tuesday and Thursday are close behind. Saturday has the fewest, with only five free mics in total.

### Do you have to buy a drink at a free open mic?

Not always, but you should. Many free mics run at bars that are giving up the room for the evening, and buying a drink is what keeps those rooms running.

## Find a free room tonight

You can browse every [free open mic](/free-mics) in New York with the night, start time and venue for each one, or see [everything running](/open-mics) by borough.

Start with [Brooklyn](/open-mics/brooklyn), [Queens](/open-mics/queens) or [Wednesday](/open-mics/wednesday).

title: What Is a Bringer Show? NYC Comedy Explained
excerpt: Bringer shows give you stage time only if you bring paying guests. What they are, what they really cost, and when they are worth doing.
metaDescription: A bringer show requires comics to bring paying guests in exchange for stage time. What they are, what they cost you, and when they are worth doing in NYC.
author: Adam Malev
body:
A bringer show is a comedy show where you only get stage time if you bring a set number of paying audience members. Usually three to five people, sometimes more. They buy tickets, they often face a two drink minimum on top, and in exchange you get five minutes on stage at a real club with a real audience.

Bringers are one of the main ways comics get stage time in New York, alongside open mics. Most new comics in NYC will be offered one within their first few months.

Whether you should say yes is more complicated than most advice admits.

## How bringer shows actually work

A producer or club books a lineup of newer comics. Each comic is told they need to bring, say, four paying guests. If you bring four, you perform. If you bring two, you might get cut, or bumped to a worse slot, or allowed up briefly as a favour.

The club fills seats it would otherwise struggle to fill. The producer gets an audience without marketing. You get stage time in front of people who are not other comedians, which is genuinely different from an open mic.

That last part is the real argument for them. At a typical open mic the room is comics waiting their turn. At a bringer the room is civilians, and material that works in front of civilians is the material that eventually gets you booked.

## What a bringer show actually costs you

The ticket price is not the cost. The cost is your friends.

If you do a bringer with four guests at twenty dollars plus a two drink minimum, you have asked four people to spend fifty or sixty dollars each on a night watching eight newer comics, most of whom they do not know. That is around two hundred dollars of other people's money to get yourself five minutes.

You can ask people to do that once. Maybe twice. The people who will come are a finite resource, and most comics burn through them in a couple of months.

The second cost is quality. A bringer audience is made of people who came to support one specific comic and have no interest in the other seven. The room is attentive during your set and restless the rest of the time, which makes for a strange night and a misleading read on your own material.

## When a bringer show is worth doing

There are real cases.

If you have never performed for a non-comic audience, doing one bringer teaches you something no open mic can. That lesson is worth the cost once.

If you want footage, a bringer gives you a club stage, decent lighting and an audience that laughs. Comics need a tape to get booked, and a tape from an open mic looks like what it is.

If the club is one you want to work at eventually, showing up and filling seats gets you known to the people who book it.

## When it is not

If a club is running bringers every week and the lineup is always different newer comics, that is a business model rather than an opportunity. You are the marketing department.

If you are being told the bringer is how you get booked properly, be sceptical. Most comics who get booked got there through open mics, producing their own shows and knowing people, not through filling seats.

If you are doing a third bringer in a month, stop. Your friends have noticed.

## The free alternative

The reason bringers work is that stage time feels scarce when you are starting. In New York it is not. There are 418 comedy open mics listed on Comediq and 128 of them are free, running every night of the week.

Doing three free mics a week costs you nothing and gets you more reps than one bringer a month ever will. Use bringers for the things open mics cannot give you, which is a real audience and a usable tape, and get your volume somewhere else.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is a bringer show in comedy?

A bringer show is a comedy show where comics are given stage time on the condition that they bring a set number of paying audience members, usually three to five. If you do not bring enough guests, you may not perform.

### Are bringer shows a scam?

Not exactly, but the exchange favours the club. You provide the audience and the club provides the stage. They are honest when disclosed upfront and a problem when they are presented as a booking opportunity rather than what they are.

### Do you get paid for a bringer show?

No. Bringer shows are unpaid. Your compensation is the stage time, and your guests pay for their own tickets and any drink minimum.

### How much does a bringer show cost?

Nothing directly for the comic. Your guests typically pay fifteen to twenty five dollars each plus a two drink minimum, so bringing four people can mean two hundred dollars of other people's money.

### Are bringer shows worth it for new comedians?

Occasionally. They are useful for performing in front of a non-comedian audience and for getting usable video. They are a poor way to build regular stage time, because the audience supply runs out fast.

### What is the difference between a bringer show and an open mic?

An open mic is free or cheap, requires no guests, and the audience is mostly other comics. A bringer requires you to supply paying guests and performs to a real audience at a club.

## Get stage time without bringing anyone

You can browse every [free open mic](/free-mics) in New York, or see [all open mics](/open-mics) by borough and night with the cost and sign-up method listed.

Start with [Brooklyn](/open-mics/brooklyn), [Queens](/open-mics/queens) or [beginner-friendly rooms](/beginner-friendly).
